column1: Enable memory-optimized storage with {{c1::MEMORY_OPTIMIZED = ON}} in the CREATE TABLE options.
column2:
SQL Server also requires a memory-optimized filegroup before table creation.
Review source

column1: For durable memory-optimized storage, use WITH (MEMORY_OPTIMIZED = ON, DURABILITY = {{c1::SCHEMA_AND_DATA}}).
column2:
Both the definition and data survive recovery under normal full durability.
Review source

column1: The memory-optimized durability option that persists only the table definition is DURABILITY = {{c1::SCHEMA_ONLY}}.
column2:
The rows are not persisted across a database restart.
Review source

column1: A system-versioned temporal table requires two period columns of type {{c1::DATETIME2}}.
column2:
The columns record the system-validity interval for each row version.
Review source

column1: Define a temporal period's start column with ValidFrom DATETIME2 GENERATED ALWAYS AS {{c1::ROW START}}.
column2:
SQL Server supplies the beginning of each row version's validity interval.
Review source

column1: Define a temporal period's end column with ValidTo DATETIME2 GENERATED ALWAYS AS {{c1::ROW END}}.
column2:
SQL Server supplies the end of each row version's validity interval.
Review source

column1: Associate temporal period columns with {{c1::PERIOD FOR SYSTEM_TIME}} (ValidFrom, ValidTo).
column2:
This clause identifies the row-start and row-end columns as the system-time period.
Review source

column1: Enable automatic temporal row versioning with WITH ({{c1::SYSTEM_VERSIONING = ON}}).
column2:
The table must also satisfy the requirements for a system-versioned temporal table.
Review source

column1: Query a temporal snapshot with SELECT * FROM dbo.Employee FOR SYSTEM_TIME {{c1::AS OF}} '2026-01-01T00:00:00';
column2:
The query returns row versions valid at the specified UTC time.
Review source

column1: In SQL Server 2017 and later, omitting a temporal table's HISTORY_RETENTION_PERIOD defaults retention to {{c1::INFINITE}}.
column2:
History does not age out automatically without a finite retention policy or another cleanup process.
Review source

column1: Define a SQL table over external data with the {{c1::CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE}} statement.
column2:
The definition describes data stored outside the database.
Review source

column1: In a SQL Server file-based external table, {{c1::LOCATION}} specifies the file or folder path within the source.
column2:
The external data source establishes the root location.
Review source

column1: The {{c1::DATA_SOURCE}} option names the external data source used by a SQL Server external table.
column2:
The referenced object establishes connectivity to the external data.
Review source

column1: The {{c1::FILE_FORMAT}} option names the external file format object used by a file-based external table.
column2:
The value references an object, not simply the word PARQUET or CSV.
Review source

column1: SQL Server ledger tables are available starting with {{c1::SQL Server 2022}}.
column2:
Ledger is also available in Azure SQL Database and Azure SQL Managed Instance.
Review source

column1: Enable an updatable ledger table with CREATE TABLE options WITH ({{c1::LEDGER = ON}}).
column2:
Without APPEND_ONLY = ON, ledger tables are updatable by default.
Review source

column1: Create append-only ledger storage with WITH (LEDGER = ON ({{c1::APPEND_ONLY = ON}})).
column2:
APPEND_ONLY belongs inside the LEDGER option's parentheses, not beside it as a separate table option.
Review source

column1: A {{c1::database digest}} is the latest ledger block's hash and represents the state of ledger data.
column2:
Protect this trusted reference outside the database for later verification.
Review source

column1: Create a graph node table with CREATE TABLE dbo.Person (PersonID INT, Name NVARCHAR(100)) {{c1::AS NODE}};
column2:
A node table stores entities with generated graph identifiers. Fabric SQL database supports graph tables, but does not mirror them to OneLake.
Review source

column1: Create a graph edge table with CREATE TABLE dbo.Knows {{c1::AS EDGE}};
column2:
An edge table stores relationships and does not require user-defined columns.
Review source

column1: The SQL Graph pseudo-column {{c1::$node_id}} uniquely identifies a node in the database.
column2:
Use the supported pseudo-column rather than internal columns with generated name suffixes.
Review source

column1: The SQL Graph pseudo-column {{c1::$edge_id}} uniquely identifies an edge in the database.
column2:
An edge identifier is distinct from the identifiers of its endpoint nodes.
Review source

column1: The SQL Graph edge pseudo-column {{c1::$from_id}} identifies the node where the edge originates.
column2:
It contains the source node's graph identifier.
Review source

column1: The SQL Graph edge pseudo-column {{c1::$to_id}} identifies the node where the edge terminates.
column2:
It contains the destination node's graph identifier.
Review source

column1: SQL Graph edges are {{c1::directed}} relationships between two nodes.
column2:
The source and destination roles are represented by $from_id and $to_id.
Review source

column1: The {{c1::MATCH}} predicate expresses SQL Graph traversal patterns in a WHERE clause.
column2:
It relates node and edge aliases through a graph pattern.
Review source
